nameStory: Schuette's hawthorn is named after a botanist who helped identify this particular species among the notoriously confusing hawthorn family. It's also called royal hawthorn, perhaps because of its stately appearance or the rich red color of its ripe fruits that might remind someone of royal jewels.
description: Schuette's hawthorn is a small, shrubby tree that belongs to the rose family, sharing ancestry with apples, cherries, and actual roses. Like its thorny cousins, it produces clusters of white flowers in spring followed by small red fruits in fall. It typically grows as a multi-stemmed shrub or small tree, forming dense thickets along woodland edges and in abandoned fields.

idTips.label: Thorns
idTips.description: Sharp, sturdy thorns stick out from branches and twigs - these can be quite painful to the touch and are one of the most reliable ways to identify any hawthorn

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Clusters of small white flowers with five petals bloom in late spring, each flower about the size of a dime with a sweet, somewhat musky fragrance

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small red berries ripen in fall, each about the size of a large pea with a dry, mealy texture when squeezed

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to egg-shaped leaves with serrated edges feel somewhat thick and leathery, arranged alternately along the branches

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a dense, often multi-stemmed shrub or small tree, creating impenetrable thorny thickets in open areas

habitat: Look for Schuette's hawthorn along forest edges where woods meet fields, and in old abandoned fields or pastures that are slowly returning to forest. It thrives in sunny to partially shaded spots with well-drained soil and often grows alongside other pioneer species like dogwoods and elderberries.

seasonality.spring: White flower clusters bloom in late spring after leaves emerge, filling the air with their distinctive sweet-musky scent.
seasonality.summer: Green fruits develop and leaves are fully expanded, making the thorny nature very apparent to anyone trying to get close.
seasonality.fall: Fruits ripen to bright red and leaves may turn yellow or orange before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Bare thorny branches and persistent red fruits make identification possible, along with the characteristic dense, shrubby growth pattern.

funFact: Hawthorns are so genetically variable and prone to hybridization that there are over 1,000 described species in North America alone - botanists joke that there are as many hawthorn species as there are botanists studying them!
confusionNotes: With only 4 recorded observations in New England, Schuette's hawthorn is extremely rare here and easily confused with the many other hawthorn species. The thorns are your best clue you're looking at a hawthorn, but distinguishing between hawthorn species often requires expert knowledge of subtle leaf and fruit differences.
contextualKnowledge: Hawthorns as a group are notoriously difficult to identify to species level - even experienced botanists struggle with them. Many field guides recommend simply identifying plants as 'hawthorn species' rather than attempting to determine the exact species without specialized training.
compareHints: Among New England's many hawthorn species, Schuette's hawthorn is distinguished by subtle characteristics that require expert identification. More commonly encountered relatives include dotted hawthorn with its spotted fruits and common hawthorn with its deeply lobed leaves. All share the characteristic thorns and white flower clusters, but differ in leaf shape, fruit details, and growth patterns.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Dotted hawthorn stands out from its many New England relatives primarily by its spotted fruits.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, common hawthorn stands out for having just one seed per fruit (most others have 2-5 seeds) and deeply lobed leaves with 3-7 divisions.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, cockspur stands out with the longest thorns - much longer than dotted hawthorn's short spines or Washington hawthorn's modest thorns.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, big-fruit hawthorn stands out for its notably larger berries and earlier bloom time.
Among New England hawthorns, large-thorn hawthorn stands out primarily for its exceptionally long, straight thorns that dwarf those of relatives like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn.

Among the many hawthorn species in New England, Washington hawthorn stands out with its distinctly triangular, deeply lobed leaves (rather than the more oval or rounded leaves of species like dotted hawthorn).
Among New England's many hawthorn species, waxy-fruited hawthorn stands out primarily for its distinctively coated berries - no other local hawthorn has that waxy, frosted appearance on the fruits.

Among New England's many hawthorns, fireberry hawthorn stands out for its golden-yellow unripe fruits - most relatives like dotted hawthorn or cockspur hawthorn have green unripe fruits that turn red.
Large-flowered cockspurthorn stands out from its many hawthorn relatives primarily by its notably large flowers - nearly twice the size of most other hawthorns.
Among New England hawthorns, fanleaf hawthorn is distinguished by its broader, more fan-shaped leaves compared to most relatives.
Among New England hawthorns, Biltmore hawthorn stands out for its green, yellow, or orange fruits - most others like dotted hawthorn, common hawthorn, and cockspur hawthorn have red fruits.

Cleft-leaved hawthorn's leaves are much more deeply divided than most New England hawthorns - while dotted hawthorn has shallow lobes and cockspur hawthorn has barely any lobes at all, this species' leaves are cut nearly to the midrib.

Among New England's hawthorns, pea hawthorn stands out for having the smallest fruits in the genus - significantly smaller than the cherry-sized fruits of dotted hawthorn or the larger berries of cockspur hawthorn.
Among New England's many hawthorns, downy hawthorn stands out for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - most others like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn have smooth or only slightly hairy leaves.
Blanchard's hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having more deeply lobed leaves and longer thorns.
Miss Jones' hawthorn is distinguished from other New England hawthorns primarily by subtle differences in leaf shape, thorn characteristics, and fruit details that require close examination.
Stone's hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having more deeply lobed leaves and different fruit characteristics.
Fleshy hawthorn stands out from its many hawthorn relatives by having the juiciest, most succulent berries in the group.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, scarlet hawthorn is distinguished by its particularly prominent thorns and bright red fruits.
Northern hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having less deeply lobed leaves and different fruit characteristics, though these distinctions can be subtle.
Dodge's hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having less prominently marked leaves and typically fewer, larger thorns.
Holmes' hawthorn is most closely related to scarlet hawthorn but distinguished by its more elongated leaves and egg-shaped rather than round fruits.
Among New England's many hawthorns, broad-leaved cockspurthorn stands out for its exceptionally broad, substantial leaves that are wider than most of its relatives.
Hairy cockspurthorn differs from its closest relative, downy hawthorn, primarily in having about 10 stamens per flower instead of 20, and the two species have separate native ranges.

Grove hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having longer thorns and less deeply cut leaves.
Keep's Hawthorn differs from common hawthorns like dotted hawthorn in subtle leaf lobe patterns and fruit characteristics that require expert knowledge to distinguish reliably.

Among New England hawthorns, poplar hawthorn stands out immediately for its broad, oval, relatively unlobed leaves - most other hawthorns like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn have deeply cut, lobed leaves.
Unlike the common red-fruited hawthorns like dotted hawthorn or cockspur hawthorn, straw-fruited hawthorn produces distinctively pale yellow berries.

Among New England's many hawthorn species, stinking hawthorn stands out for its yellow-green fruits with red markings rather than the solid red fruits of most others like dotted hawthorn or cockspur hawthorn.
